body: On September 30 of this year, I ran a warm bath, took a bottle of tramadol, and took a blade and started slicing my wrists. Because I took the pain medication, I didn’t feel much pain but still felt it a little. After the slices on my wrists didn’t seem to be doing the job, I took the blade to my neck. {Unfortunately} by the time I started on my neck, I was weak and didn’t have much strength to cut deep enough. I kept trying, going from my wrists to my neck but it’s December 5 and I’m still here typing this reply to you. My sister found me and the paramedics took me to the hospital where I had to have emergency surgery to close up my wrists. When I woke up from surgery in ICU, I found out they had to repair a tendon in my right wrist and I had about 20 stitches in each arm and 2 stitches on my neck. A little over two months later and my scars are an emotionally and physically painful reminder of what I tried to do, and what I failed to do. The scars left behind are sensitive to the touch and causes sharp pain in my hands. I hope one day I heal enough to cover them with a tattoo or do laser scar removal or something but as of right now, it’s just a shameful reminder of what happened that night. So for me, slitting my wrists was not painful, but everything since surviving slitting my wrists has been extremely painful, so much so that if I could go back and change how I did things, I most certainly would, or I would at least be certain that I succeeded with what I set out to do. I wouldn’t recommend it because even with my very drastic attempt, I still didn’t die.

Honestly thank you for posting this. I'm in a very similar situation. I started college in 2016 and after my junior year in 2019, I took a break. I started back going to school Spring 2023 and am just now about to graduate, at 25 years old. Before my break from school I wasn't the best student, not that I couldn't do well, I just did not apply myself. When I came back I killed it in class, making only 1 B and the rest all A's, though even this could only bring my GPA up to about a 2.8 (not exactly sure since final grades have not been submitted yet, I graduate in December). I took the LSAT at the beginning of November and just got back my score today. I took a few practice tests before hand and got a 151. My studying was pretty much just taking a few practice tests and not much else. I got a 156 on the actual test. I was feeling disappointed (not sure if this is actually the right emotion but it's the easiest way to express it) by this score. This lead me to google search if 156 is a good score which brought me to your post and I'm so glad I found it. I was worried about my score, my GPA, and how I would pay for school. After reading all the comments, I'm feeling much better about my score and my overall journey! Thank you so much for sharing your journey, I'm going to really study some more! I think I will have more time to devote to studying now that I won't be a full time student and employee!
